user_input: In DRF, when exactly do the authentication classes run relative to the rest of my view logic?
reference: Authentication is the very first thing a DRF view does. It runs before the permission and throttling checks and before any of your own view code.
reference_contexts: Authentication always runs at the very start of the view, before the permission and throttling checks occur, and before any other code is allowed to proceed.
llm_response: Authentication classes run at the very start of the view. They execute before permission and throttling checks occur, and before any other code is allowed to proceed.
llm_references:
Authentication - Django REST framework

Authentication

Auth needs to be pluggable.
— Jacob Kaplan-Moss,
"REST worst practices" (https://jacobian.org/writing/rest-worst-practices/)

Authentication is the mechanism of associating an incoming request with a set of identifying credentials, such as the user the request came from, or the token that it was signed with.  The
permission (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/permissions/)
and
throttling (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/throttling/)
policies can then use those credentials to determine if the request should be permitted.

REST framework provides several authentication schemes out of the box, and also allows you to implement custom schemes.

Authentication always runs at the very start of the view, before the permission and throttling checks occur, and before any other code is allowed to proceed.

The
`request.user`
property will typically be set to an instance of the
`contrib.auth`
package's
`User`
class.

The
`request.auth`
property is used for any additional authentication information, for example, it may be used to represent an authentication token that the request was signed with.

Note
Don't forget that
authentication by itself won't allow or disallow an incoming request
, it simply identifies the credentials that the request was made with.
For information on how to set up the permission policies for your API please see the
permissions documentation (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/permissions/)
.

The authentication schemes are always defined as a list of classes.  REST framework will attempt to authenticate with each class in the list, and will set
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
using the return value of the first class that successfully authenticates.

If no class authenticates,
`request.user`
will be set to an instance of
`django.contrib.auth.models.AnonymousUser`
, and
`request.auth`
will be set to
`None`
.

The value of
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
for unauthenticated requests can be modified using the
`UNAUTHENTICATED_USER`
and
`UNAUTHENTICATED_TOKEN`
settings.

user_input: Coming from plain Django I keep hunting for some kind of "login middleware" I can switch on so the whole API requires auth — but there doesn't seem to be one. What's the DRF way to set the authentication for every endpoint at once?
reference: Set them globally with DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES in your REST_FRAMEWORK settings dict; every view uses that default unless it overrides it per-view or per-viewset.
reference_contexts: The default authentication schemes may be set globally, using the DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES setting.

REST_FRAMEWORK = { 'DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES' : [ 'rest_framework.authentication.BasicAuthentication' , 'rest_framework.authentication.SessionAuthentication' , ] } You can also set the authentication scheme on a per-view or per-viewset basis, using the APIView class-based views.
llm_response:
To require authentication for every endpoint in your API, you should use the global `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES` setting.

### The Recommended Approach
Set the global permission policy in your `settings.py` file to use `IsAuthenticated`:

```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES': [
        'rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated',
    ]
}
```

This ensures that permission checks are run at the start of every view, granting access only to authenticated users and returning a 401 status code for unauthenticated requests.

### Additional Considerations
*   **Authentication Schemes:** While `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES` enforces the requirement, you must also ensure your API has valid authentication schemes configured. You can set these globally in `settings.py` using `DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`:
    ```python
    REST_FRAMEWORK = {
        'DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES': [
            'rest_framework.authentication.BasicAuthentication',
            'rest_framework.authentication.SessionAuthentication',
        ],
        'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES': [
            'rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated',
        ]
    }
    ```
*   **Per-View Overrides:** If you need to deviate from the global policy for specific endpoints, you can override the settings on a per-view basis. Using `APIView` classes or the `@api_view` decorator, you can define `permission_classes` and `authentication_classes` attributes. Note that setting these on a view causes that view to ignore the global defaults defined in `settings.py`.
*   **Middleware:** Do not rely on Django's `LoginRequiredMiddleware`. DRF views are opted-out of this middleware because DRF handles authentication and permissions internally, and the middleware's redirect behavior is not suitable for API requests.
llm_references:
The default permission policy may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`
setting.  For example.

```
`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES':['rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated',]}`
```

If not specified, this setting defaults to allowing unrestricted access:

```
`'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES':['rest_framework.permissions.AllowAny',]`
```

You can also set the authentication policy on a per-view, or per-viewset basis,
using the
`APIView`
class-based views.

```
`fromrest_framework.permissionsimportIsAuthenticatedfromrest_framework.responseimportResponsefromrest_framework.viewsimportAPIViewclassExampleView(APIView):permission_classes=[IsAuthenticated]defget(self,request,format=None):content={'status':'request was permitted'}returnResponse(content)`
```

Or, if you're using the
`@api_view`
decorator with function based views.

```
`fromrest_framework.decoratorsimportapi_view,permission_classesfromrest_framework.permissionsimportIsAuthenticatedfromrest_framework.responseimportResponse@api_view(['GET'])@permission_classes([IsAuthenticated])defexample_view(request,format=None):content={'status':'request was permitted'}returnResponse(content)`
```

Note
When you set new permission classes via the class attribute or decorators you're telling the view to ignore the default list set in the
`settings.py`
file.

Provided they inherit from
`rest_framework.permissions.BasePermission`
, permissions can be composed using standard Python bitwise operators. For example,
`IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`
could be written:

```
`fromrest_framework.permissionsimportBasePermission,IsAuthenticated,SAFE_METHODSfromrest_framework.responseimportResponsefromrest_framework.viewsimportAPIViewclassReadOnly(BasePermission):defhas_permission(self,request,view):returnrequest.methodinSAFE_METHODSclassExampleView(APIView):permission_classes=[IsAuthenticated|ReadOnly]defget(self,request,format=None):content={'status':'request was permitted'}returnResponse(content)`
```

Note
Composition of permissions supports the
`&`
(and),
`|`
(or) and
`~`
(not) operators, and also allows the use of brackets
`(`
`)`
to group expressions.
Operators follow the same precedence and associativity rules as standard logical operators (
`~`
highest, then
`&`
, then
`|`
).

If you're running Django 5.1+ and use the
LoginRequiredMiddleware (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/middleware/#django.contrib.auth.middleware.LoginRequiredMiddleware)
, please note that all views from DRF are opted-out of this middleware.  This is because the authentication in DRF is based on authentication and permissions classes, which may be determined after the middleware has been applied.  Additionally, when the request is not authenticated, the middleware redirects the user to the login page, which is not suitable for API requests, where it's preferable to return a 401 status code.

REST framework offers an equivalent mechanism for DRF views via the global settings,
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
and
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`
.  They should be changed accordingly if you need to enforce that API requests are logged in.

The default authentication schemes may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
setting.  For example.

```
`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES':['rest_framework.authentication.BasicAuthentication','rest_framework.authentication.SessionAuthentication',]}`
```

You can also set the authentication scheme on a per-view or per-viewset basis,
using the
`APIView`
class-based views.

```
`fromrest_framework.authenticationimportSessionAuthentication,BasicAuthenticationfromrest_framework.permissionsimportIsAuthenticatedfromrest_framework.responseimportResponsefromrest_framework.viewsimportAPIViewclassExampleView(APIView):authentication_classes=[SessionAuthentication,BasicAuthentication]permission_classes=[IsAuthenticated]defget(self,request,format=None):content={'user':str(request.user),# `django.contrib.auth.User` instance.'auth':str(request.auth),# None}returnResponse(content)`
```

Or, if you're using the
`@api_view`
decorator with function based views.

```
`@api_view(['GET'])@authentication_classes([SessionAuthentication,BasicAuthentication])@permission_classes([IsAuthenticated])defexample_view(request,format=None):content={'user':str(request.user),# `django.contrib.auth.User` instance.'auth':str(request.auth),# None}returnResponse(content)`
```

Authentication or identification by itself is not usually sufficient to gain access to information or code.  For that, the entity requesting access must have authorization.
—
Apple Developer Documentation (https://developer.apple.com/library/mac/#documentation/security/Conceptual/AuthenticationAndAuthorizationGuide/Authorization/Authorization.html)

Together with
authentication (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/authentication/)
and
throttling (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/throttling/)
, permissions determine whether a request should be granted or denied access.

Permission checks are always run at the very start of the view, before any other code is allowed to proceed.  Permission checks will typically use the authentication information in the
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
properties to determine if the incoming request should be permitted.

Permissions are used to grant or deny access for different classes of users to different parts of the API.

The simplest style of permission would be to allow access to any authenticated user, and deny access to any unauthenticated user. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticated`
class in REST framework.

A slightly less strict style of permission would be to allow full access to authenticated users, but allow read-only access to unauthenticated users. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`
class in REST framework.

user_input: What header and prefix does DRF's built-in TokenAuthentication expect for the token?
reference: Send it in the Authorization header prefixed with the literal word "Token" and a space, e.g. `Authorization: Token 9944...`. Subclass TokenAuthentication if you'd rather use a keyword like Bearer.
reference_contexts: key ) For clients to authenticate, the token key should be included in the Authorization HTTP header.

For example: Authorization : Token 9944b09199c62bcf9418ad846dd0e4bbdfc6ee4b If you want to use a different keyword in the header, such as Bearer , simply subclass TokenAuthentication and set the keyword class variable.
llm_response:
DRF's built-in `TokenAuthentication` expects the token to be included in the `Authorization` HTTP header. The token key must be prefixed by the string literal "Token", followed by a space.

Example format:
`Authorization: Token 9944b09199c62bcf9418ad846dd0e4bbdfc6ee4b`

If you wish to use a different keyword (such as `Bearer`), you can subclass `TokenAuthentication` and set the `keyword` class variable.
llm_references:
Note
The token authentication provided by Django REST framework is a fairly simple implementation.
For an implementation which allows more than one token per user, has some tighter security implementation details, and supports token expiry, please see the
Django REST Knox (https://github.com/James1345/django-rest-knox)
third party package.

This authentication scheme uses a simple token-based HTTP Authentication scheme.  Token authentication is appropriate for client-server setups, such as native desktop and mobile clients.

To use the
`TokenAuthentication`
scheme you'll need to
configure the authentication classes (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/authentication/#setting-the-authentication-scheme)
to include
`TokenAuthentication`
, and additionally include
`rest_framework.authtoken`
in your
`INSTALLED_APPS`
setting:

```
`INSTALLED_APPS=[...'rest_framework.authtoken']`
```

Make sure to run
`manage.py migrate`
after changing your settings.

The
`rest_framework.authtoken`
app provides Django database migrations.

You'll also need to create tokens for your users.

```
`fromrest_framework.authtoken.modelsimportTokentoken=Token.objects.create(user=...)print(token.key)`
```

For clients to authenticate, the token key should be included in the
`Authorization`
HTTP header.  The key should be prefixed by the string literal "Token", with whitespace separating the two strings.  For example:

```
`Authorization:Token9944b09199c62bcf9418ad846dd0e4bbdfc6ee4b`
```

If you want to use a different keyword in the header, such as
`Bearer`
, simply subclass
`TokenAuthentication`
and set the
`keyword`
class variable.

If successfully authenticated,
`TokenAuthentication`
provides the following credentials.

`request.user`
will be a Django
`User`
instance.
`request.auth`
will be a
`rest_framework.authtoken.models.Token`
instance.

Unauthenticated responses that are denied permission will result in an
`HTTP 401 Unauthorized`
response with an appropriate WWW-Authenticate header.  For example:

```
`WWW-Authenticate:Token`
```

The
`curl`
command line tool may be useful for testing token authenticated APIs.  For example:

```
`curl-X GET http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/example/ -H 'Authorization: Token 9944b09199c62bcf9418ad846dd0e4bbdfc6ee4b'`
```

Note
If you use
`TokenAuthentication`
in production you must ensure that your API is only available over
`https`
.

user_input: Which permission class gives anonymous users read access but requires login to write?
reference: IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly: authenticated users can make any request, while unauthenticated users are limited to the safe methods GET, HEAD and OPTIONS.
reference_contexts: The IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly will allow authenticated users to perform any request.
This permission is suitable if you want to your API to allow read permissions to anonymous users, and only allow write permissions to authenticated users.
llm_response:
The permission class that allows anonymous users read access while requiring login for write access is `IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`.

This class ensures that authenticated requests receive read-write access, while unauthenticated requests are restricted to "safe" methods (`GET`, `HEAD`, or `OPTIONS`). 

To implement this, you must:
1. Import the permissions module: `from rest_framework import permissions`
2. Add the following property to your view classes: `permission_classes = [permissions.IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly]`

user_input: What's the difference between IsAuthenticated and AllowAny?
reference: IsAuthenticated blocks anonymous users and lets logged-in users through; AllowAny lets every request through regardless of authentication.
reference_contexts: The IsAuthenticated permission class will deny permission to any unauthenticated user, and allow permission otherwise.
The AllowAny permission class will allow unrestricted access, regardless of if the request was authenticated or unauthenticated .
llm_response:
The difference between `AllowAny` and `IsAuthenticated` is as follows:

*   **`AllowAny`**: Allows unrestricted access to the API, regardless of whether the user is authenticated or unauthenticated [1].
*   **`IsAuthenticated`**: Denies access to any unauthenticated user and allows access to registered (authenticated) users [2]. This is the appropriate choice if you want your API to be accessible only to registered users [2].
llm_references:
The
`AllowAny`
permission class will allow unrestricted access,
regardless of if the request was authenticated or unauthenticated
.

This permission is not strictly required, since you can achieve the same result by using an empty list or tuple for the permissions setting, but you may find it useful to specify this class because it makes the intention explicit.

The
`IsAuthenticated`
permission class will deny permission to any unauthenticated user, and allow permission otherwise.

This permission is suitable if you want your API to only be accessible to registered users.

user_input: How do I turn on pagination for my whole API, and what settings does it need?
reference: Set DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS and PAGE_SIZE globally in REST_FRAMEWORK. You need both — they're None by default.
reference_contexts: The pagination style may be set globally, using the DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS and PAGE_SIZE setting keys.

For example, to use the built-in limit/offset pagination, you would do something like this: REST_FRAMEWORK = { 'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS' : 'rest_framework.pagination.LimitOffsetPagination' , 'PAGE_SIZE' : 100 } Note that you need to set both the pagination class, and the page size that should be used.
llm_response:
To turn on pagination for your whole API, you must configure the `REST_FRAMEWORK` setting in your project's settings file. You are required to set both the `DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS` and the `PAGE_SIZE`.

### Required Settings
You must define the following keys within your `REST_FRAMEWORK` dictionary:
*   **`DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS`**: The path to the pagination class you wish to use (e.g., `'rest_framework.pagination.PageNumberPagination'`).
*   **`PAGE_SIZE`**: An integer representing the number of items per page.

### Example Configuration
To use the built-in `PageNumberPagination` globally:
```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS': 'rest_framework.pagination.PageNumberPagination',
    'PAGE_SIZE': 100
}
```

### Available Pagination Styles
You can choose from the following built-in classes for the `DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS`:
1.  **`rest_framework.pagination.PageNumberPagination`**: Uses a `page` query parameter by default.
2.  **`rest_framework.pagination.LimitOffsetPagination`**: Uses `limit` and `offset` query parameters. If `PAGE_SIZE` is set, the `limit` parameter becomes optional.
3.  **`rest_framework.pagination.CursorPagination`**: Uses an opaque cursor for pagination.

### Important Considerations
*   **Automatic vs. Manual**: Pagination is performed automatically only if you are using generic views or viewsets. If you are using a regular `APIView`, you must call the pagination API yourself.
*   **Customization**: If you need to modify aspects like the query parameter name (e.g., changing `page` to `p`), you must create a subclass of one of the pagination classes, override the desired attributes, and point `DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS` to your custom class path.
*   **Disabling**: Pagination can be turned off for specific views by setting the `pagination_class` attribute to `None`.
llm_references: Pagination - Django REST framework

The pagination style may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS`
and
`PAGE_SIZE`
setting keys. For example, to use the built-in limit/offset pagination, you would do something like this:

```
`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.LimitOffsetPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`
```

Note that you need to set both the pagination class, and the page size that should be used.  Both
`DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS`
and
`PAGE_SIZE`
are
`None`
by default.

You can also set the pagination class on an individual view by using the
`pagination_class`
attribute. Typically you'll want to use the same pagination style throughout your API, although you might want to vary individual aspects of the pagination, such as default or maximum page size, on a per-view basis.

If you want to modify particular aspects of the pagination style, you'll want to override one of the pagination classes, and set the attributes that you want to change.

```
`classLargeResultsSetPagination(PageNumberPagination):page_size=1000page_size_query_param='page_size'max_page_size=10000classStandardResultsSetPagination(PageNumberPagination):page_size=100page_size_query_param='page_size'max_page_size=1000`
```

You can then apply your new style to a view using the
`pagination_class`
attribute:

```
`classBillingRecordsView(generics.ListAPIView):queryset=Billing.objects.all()serializer_class=BillingRecordsSerializerpagination_class=LargeResultsSetPagination`
```

Or apply the style globally, using the
`DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS`
settings key. For example:

```
`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'apps.core.pagination.StandardResultsSetPagination'}`
```

To enable the
`CursorPagination`
style globally, use the following configuration, modifying the
`PAGE_SIZE`
as desired:

```
`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.CursorPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`
```

On
`GenericAPIView`
subclasses you may also set the
`pagination_class`
attribute to select
`CursorPagination`
on a per-view basis.

To enable the
`LimitOffsetPagination`
style globally, use the following configuration:

```
`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.LimitOffsetPagination'}`
```

Optionally, you may also set a
`PAGE_SIZE`
key. If the
`PAGE_SIZE`
parameter is also used then the
`limit`
query parameter will be optional, and may be omitted by the client.

On
`GenericAPIView`
subclasses you may also set the
`pagination_class`
attribute to select
`LimitOffsetPagination`
on a per-view basis.

To enable the
`PageNumberPagination`
style globally, use the following configuration, and set the
`PAGE_SIZE`
as desired:

```
`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.PageNumberPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`
```

On
`GenericAPIView`
subclasses you may also set the
`pagination_class`
attribute to select
`PageNumberPagination`
on a per-view basis.

By default, the query parameter name used for pagination is
`page`
.
This can be customized by subclassing
`PageNumberPagination`
and overriding the
`page_query_param`
attribute.

For example:

```
`fromrest_framework.paginationimportPageNumberPaginationclassCustomPagination(PageNumberPagination):page_query_param='p'`
```

With this configuration, clients would request pages using
`?p=2`
instead of
`?page=2`
.

Django provides a few classes that help you manage paginated data – that is, data that’s split across several pages, with “Previous/Next” links.
—
Django documentation (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/pagination/)

REST framework includes support for customizable pagination styles. This allows you to modify how large result sets are split into individual pages of data.

The pagination API can support either:

Pagination links that are provided as part of the content of the response.
Pagination links that are included in response headers, such as
`Content-Range`
or
`Link`
.

The built-in styles currently all use links included as part of the content of the response. This style is more accessible when using the browsable API.

Pagination is only performed automatically if you're using the generic views or viewsets. If you're using a regular
`APIView`
, you'll need to call into the pagination API yourself to ensure you return a paginated response. See the source code for the
`mixins.ListModelMixin`
and
`generics.GenericAPIView`
classes for an example.

Pagination can be turned off by setting the pagination class to
`None`
.

user_input: Once a list endpoint is paginated, what does the response body actually look like — how is a client supposed to know how many records exist in total and where to get the next batch?
reference: The results get wrapped in an envelope rather than returned as a bare array. A page-number paginated response carries `count` (the total number of records across all pages), `next` and `previous` (full URLs to the adjacent pages, or null at either end), and `results` (the records for this page). Clients walk the collection by following `next` until it comes back null, rather than by computing page numbers themselves.
reference_contexts: HTTP 200 OK { "count": 1023, "next": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=5", "previous": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=3", "results": [ ... ] }
llm_response:
When a list endpoint is paginated, the response body is a JSON object containing the following keys:

*   **`count`**: The total number of records available across all pages.
*   **`next`**: A URL string pointing to the next batch of results (or `null` if there is no next page).
*   **`previous`**: A URL string pointing to the previous batch of results (or `null` if there is no previous page).
*   **`results`**: An array containing the actual data records for the current page.

The specific structure is illustrated in the following examples:

**For `PageNumberPagination`:**
```json
{
    "count": 1023,
    "next": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=5",
    "previous": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=3",
    "results": [...]
}
```

**For `LimitOffsetPagination`:**
```json
{
    "count": 1023,
    "next": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=500",
    "previous": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=300",
    "results": [...]
}
```

Note that `CursorPagination` also provides `next` and `previous` links for navigation, but it uses an opaque cursor indicator rather than page numbers or offsets to determine the position in the result set.
llm_references: Pagination - Django REST framework

This pagination style mirrors the syntax used when looking up multiple database records. The client includes both a "limit" and an
"offset" query parameter. The limit indicates the maximum number of items to return, and is equivalent to the
`page_size`
in other styles. The offset indicates the starting position of the query in relation to the complete set of unpaginated items.

Request
:

```
`GET https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=400`
```

Response
:

```
`HTTP200OK{"count":1023,"next":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=500","previous":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=300","results":[…]}`
```

This pagination style accepts a single number page number in the request query parameters.

Request
:

```
`GET https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=4`
```

Response
:

```
`HTTP200OK{"count":1023,"next":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=5","previous":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=3","results":[…]}`
```

The cursor-based pagination presents an opaque "cursor" indicator that the client may use to page through the result set. This pagination style only presents forward and reverse controls, and does not allow the client to navigate to arbitrary positions.

Cursor based pagination requires that there is a unique, unchanging ordering of items in the result set. This ordering might typically be a creation timestamp on the records, as this presents a consistent ordering to paginate against.

Cursor based pagination is more complex than other schemes. It also requires that the result set presents a fixed ordering, and does not allow the client to arbitrarily index into the result set. However it does provide the following benefits:

Provides a consistent pagination view. When used properly
`CursorPagination`
ensures that the client will never see the same item twice when paging through records, even when new items are being inserted by other clients during the pagination process.
Supports usage with very large datasets. With extremely large datasets pagination using offset-based pagination styles may become inefficient or unusable. Cursor based pagination schemes instead have fixed-time properties, and do not slow down as the dataset size increases.

user_input: What do I set so clients can search my list endpoint with ?search=?
reference: Add DRF's SearchFilter to the view and give it a search_fields attribute; the filter only activates once search_fields is set.
reference_contexts: When in use, the browsable API will include a SearchFilter control: The SearchFilter class will only be applied if the view has a search_fields attribute set.
The search_fields attribute should be a list of names of text type fields on the model, such as CharField or TextField .
llm_response:
To enable searching on your list endpoint using the `?search=` query parameter, you must perform the following steps:

1.  **Add the filter backend**: Include `filters.SearchFilter` in the `filter_backends` attribute of your view.
2.  **Define search fields**: Set the `search_fields` attribute on your view to a list of the model's text fields (e.g., `CharField` or `TextField`) that you want to be searchable.

**Example implementation:**

```python
from rest_framework import filters, generics

class UserListView(generics.ListAPIView):
    queryset = User.objects.all()
    serializer_class = UserSerializer
    filter_backends = [filters.SearchFilter]
    search_fields = ['username', 'email']
```

**Additional configuration notes:**
*   **Customizing the parameter name**: While the default query parameter is `'search'`, you can override this globally by setting `SEARCH_PARAM` in your `REST_FRAMEWORK` configuration.
*   **Search behavior**: You can change the search lookup (e.g., to exact matches or starts-with) by prefixing the field names in `search_fields` with specific characters like `=` (for `iexact`) or `^` (for `istartswith`).
*   **Related lookups**: You can search across relationships or within `JSONField`/`HStoreField` structures using the double-underscore (`__`) notation in your `search_fields` list.

user_input: How do I let clients order list results but restrict which fields they can sort on?
reference: Use OrderingFilter and set an explicit ordering_fields list on the view so users can't sort on sensitive columns.
reference_contexts: It's recommended that you explicitly specify which fields the API should allow in the ordering filter.
You can do this by setting an ordering_fields attribute on the view, like so: class UserListView ( generics .
llm_response:
To allow clients to order list results while restricting the fields they can sort on, use the `OrderingFilter` class and explicitly define the allowed fields.

### Implementation
1. Add `filters.OrderingFilter` to the `filter_backends` list in your view.
2. Set the `ordering_fields` attribute on your view to a list of the specific fields you want to permit.

**Example:**
```python
class UserListView(generics.ListAPIView):
    queryset = User.objects.all()
    serializer_class = UserSerializer
    filter_backends = [filters.OrderingFilter]
    ordering_fields = ['username', 'email']
```

### How clients use it
Clients can order results by using the `'ordering'` query parameter (or the value defined in your `ORDERING_PARAM` setting).
* **Standard order:** `?ordering=username`
* **Reverse order:** Prefix the field with a hyphen, e.g., `?ordering=-username`
* **Multiple fields:** Separate fields with commas, e.g., `?ordering=account,username`

### Notes
* **Security:** Explicitly specifying `ordering_fields` is the recommended approach to prevent data leakage, such as allowing users to sort by sensitive fields like password hashes.
* **Default behavior:** If you do not specify `ordering_fields`, the filter defaults to allowing ordering on any readable field in the `serializer_class`.
* **Allowing all fields:** If you are confident there is no sensitive data, you can set `ordering_fields = '__all__'` to allow ordering on any model field or queryset aggregate.

`ordering_fields`
attribute on the view, like so:

```
`classUserListView(generics.ListAPIView):queryset=User.objects.all()serializer_class=UserSerializerfilter_backends=[filters.OrderingFilter]ordering_fields=['username','email']`
```

This helps prevent unexpected data leakage, such as allowing users to order against a password hash field or other sensitive data.

If you
don't
specify an
`ordering_fields`
attribute on the view, the filter class will default to allowing the user to filter on any readable fields on the serializer specified by the
`serializer_class`
attribute.

If you are confident that the queryset being used by the view doesn't contain any sensitive data, you can also explicitly specify that a view should allow ordering on
any
model field or queryset aggregate, by using the special value

```
`classBookingsListView(generics.ListAPIView):queryset=Booking.objects.all()serializer_class=BookingSerializerfilter_backends=[filters.OrderingFilter]ordering_fields='__all__'`
```

`'ordering'`

user_input: I've got a Spring background and I'm looking for DRF's equivalent of a DTO — something to turn a list of model objects into JSON in one shot. How do I serialize a whole queryset at once?
reference: Pass many=True when instantiating the serializer, then give it the queryset or list of objects.
reference_contexts: To serialize a queryset or list of objects instead of a single object instance, you should pass the many=True flag when instantiating the serializer.
llm_response:
To serialize a queryset or a list of objects into JSON in one shot, you should pass the `many=True` flag when instantiating your serializer.

When you pass `many=True`, Django REST framework automatically creates a `ListSerializer` instance to handle the collection.

### Implementation Example
If you have a `BookSerializer` and a queryset, you can serialize the entire list as follows:

```python
queryset = Book.objects.all()
serializer = BookSerializer(queryset, many=True)
serializer.data
```

### Recommended Approach
*   **`ModelSerializer`**: Use this class as a shortcut if you want to automatically generate serializer fields that correspond to your Django model fields.
*   **`Serializer`**: Use this base class if you require more manual control over the output.

Both classes support the `many=True` flag for handling multiple objects.

### Additional Configuration
When using `many=True`, you can optionally pass the following arguments to the serializer to control list validation:
*   **`allow_empty`**: Defaults to `True`; set to `False` to disallow empty lists.
*   **`max_length`**: Set to a positive integer to limit the number of elements in the list.
*   **`min_length`**: Set to a positive integer to ensure the list contains at least that many elements.

`ListSerializer`
class provides the behavior for serializing and validating multiple objects at once. You won't
typically
need to use
`ListSerializer`
directly, but should instead simply pass
`many=True`
when instantiating a serializer.

When a serializer is instantiated and
`many=True`
is passed, a
`ListSerializer`
instance will be created. The serializer class then becomes a child of the parent
`ListSerializer`

The following argument can also be passed to a
`ListSerializer`
field or a serializer that is passed
`many=True`
:

`allow_empty`
: this is
`True`
by default, but can be set to
`False`
if you want to disallow empty lists as valid input.
`max_length`
: this is
`None`
by default, but can be set to a positive integer if you want to validate that the list contains no more than this number of elements.
`min_length`
: this is
`None`
by default, but can be set to a positive integer if you want to validate that the list contains no fewer than this number of elements.

The
`Serializer`
class can also handle serializing or deserializing lists of objects.

To serialize a queryset or list of objects instead of a single object instance, you should pass the
`many=True`
flag when instantiating the serializer.  You can then pass a queryset or list of objects to be serialized.

```
`queryset=Book.objects.all()serializer=BookSerializer(queryset,many=True)serializer.data# [#     {'id': 0, 'title': 'The electric kool-aid acid test', 'author': 'Tom Wolfe'},#     {'id': 1, 'title': 'If this is a man', 'author': 'Primo Levi'},#     {'id': 2, 'title': 'The wind-up bird chronicle', 'author': 'Haruki Murakami'}# ]`
```

Serializers - Django REST framework

Serializers

Expanding the usefulness of the serializers is something that we would
like to address.  However, it's not a trivial problem, and it
will take some serious design work.
— Russell Keith-Magee,
Django users group (https://groups.google.com/d/topic/django-users/sVFaOfQi4wY/discussion)

Serializers allow complex data such as querysets and model instances to be converted to native Python datatypes that can then be easily rendered into
`JSON`
,
`XML`
or other content types.  Serializers also provide deserialization, allowing parsed data to be converted back into complex types, after first validating the incoming data.

The serializers in REST framework work very similarly to Django's
`Form`
and
`ModelForm`
classes. We provide a
`Serializer`
class which gives you a powerful, generic way to control the output of your responses, as well as a
`ModelSerializer`
class which provides a useful shortcut for creating serializers that deal with model instances and querysets.

Often you'll want serializer classes that map closely to Django model definitions.

The
`ModelSerializer`
class provides a shortcut that lets you automatically create a
`Serializer`
class with fields that correspond to the Model fields.

The
`ModelSerializer`
class is the same as a regular
`Serializer`
class, except that
:

It will automatically generate a set of fields for you, based on the model.
It will automatically generate validators for the serializer, such as unique_together validators.
It includes simple default implementations of
`.create()`
and
`.update()`
.

Declaring a
`ModelSerializer`
looks like this:

```
`classAccountSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):classMeta:model=Accountfields=['id','account_name','users','created']`
```

By default, all the model fields on the class will be mapped to a corresponding serializer fields.

Any relationships such as foreign keys on the model will be mapped to
`PrimaryKeyRelatedField`
. Reverse relationships are not included by default unless explicitly included as specified in the
serializer relations (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/relations/)
documentation.

user_input: Instead of marking every field read_only=True individually on my ModelSerializer, is there a shortcut?
reference: Yes — use the Meta option read_only_fields with a list/tuple of field names.
reference_contexts: You may wish to specify multiple fields as read-only.

ModelSerializer ): class Meta : model = Account fields = [ 'id' , 'account_name' , 'users' , 'created' ] read_only_fields = [ 'account_name' ] Model fields which have editable=False set, and AutoField fields will be set to read-only by default, and do not need to be added to the read_only_fields option.
llm_response:
Yes, you can use the `read_only_fields` shortcut in the `Meta` class of your `ModelSerializer`. This option accepts a list or tuple of field names.

Example usage:

```python
class AccountSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    class Meta:
        model = Account
        fields = ['id', 'account_name', 'users', 'created']
        read_only_fields = ['account_name']
```

Additionally, note that `AutoField` fields and model fields with `editable=False` are set to read-only by default and do not need to be included in `read_only_fields`.

**Exception:** If a read-only field is part of a `unique_together` constraint, you must specify the field explicitly on the serializer with `read_only=True` and a `default` value (such as `serializers.CurrentUserDefault()`) to ensure validation works correctly.

You may wish to specify multiple fields as read-only. Instead of adding each field explicitly with the
`read_only=True`
attribute, you may use the shortcut Meta option,
`read_only_fields`

This option should be a list or tuple of field names, and is declared as follows:

```
`classAccountSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):classMeta:model=Accountfields=['id','account_name','users','created']read_only_fields=['account_name']`
```

Model fields which have
`editable=False`
set, and
`AutoField`
fields will be set to read-only by default, and do not need to be added to the
`read_only_fields`

There is a special-case where a read-only field is part of a

constraint at the model level. In this case the field is required by the serializer class in order to validate the constraint, but should also not be editable by the user.
The right way to deal with this is to specify the field explicitly on the serializer, providing both the
`read_only=True`

One example of this is a read-only relation to the currently authenticated
`User`

`unique_together`

```
`user=serializers.PrimaryKeyRelatedField(read_only=True,default=serializers.CurrentUserDefault())`
```

for details on the
UniqueTogetherValidator (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/validators/#uniquetogethervalidator)

user_input: Where do I put validation for a single serializer field?
reference: Add a .validate_<field_name> method to your Serializer subclass — it works like Django forms' .clean_<field_name> and gets the field value.
reference_contexts: You can specify custom field-level validation by adding .validate_<field_name> methods to your Serializer subclass.
llm_response:
You can validate a single serializer field using one of the following two approaches:

### 1. Field-level validation methods
You can add a `.validate_<field_name>` method to your `Serializer` subclass. This method takes the field value as an argument and must return the validated value or raise a `serializers.ValidationError`.

*   **Note:** If the field is declared with `required=False`, this validation step will not occur if the field is not included in the data.

**Example:**
```python
class BlogPostSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    title = serializers.CharField(max_length=100)

    def validate_title(self, value):
        if 'django' not in value.lower():
            raise serializers.ValidationError("Blog post is not about Django")
        return value
```

### 2. Declaring validators on the field instance
You can include validators directly on the field instance by using the `validators` argument. A validator can be any callable (such as a function) that raises a `serializers.ValidationError` on failure.

**Example:**
```python
def multiple_of_ten(value):
    if value % 10 != 0:
        raise serializers.ValidationError('Not a multiple of ten')

class GameRecord(serializers.Serializer):
    score = serializers.IntegerField(validators=[multiple_of_ten])
```

You can use any of Django's existing validators, or write your own custom validators.

user_input: In tests, how do I authenticate a request without the real credential flow?
reference: Use force_authenticate() to directly authenticate the request against a user (and optionally a token).
reference_contexts: To forcibly authenticate a request, use the force_authenticate() method.
llm_response:
To authenticate a request in tests without the real credential flow, you can use the `force_authenticate()` method. The approach depends on whether you are using `APIRequestFactory` or `APIClient`:

### Using `APIRequestFactory`
When using `APIRequestFactory`, you apply `force_authenticate` to the individual request object:

```python
from rest_framework.test import force_authenticate
factory = APIRequestFactory()
user = User.objects.get(username='olivia')
request = factory.get('/accounts/django-superstars/')

# Authenticate with user
force_authenticate(request, user=user)

# Authenticate with user and token
force_authenticate(request, user=user, token=user.auth_token)
```

### Using `APIClient`
When using `APIClient`, you can force all subsequent requests to be treated as authenticated by calling `force_authenticate` on the client instance:

```python
client = APIClient()
user = User.objects.get(username='lauren')

# Force authentication for all requests
client.force_authenticate(user=user)

# To unauthenticate subsequent requests
client.force_authenticate(user=None)
```

**Important Considerations:**
* **`APIRequestFactory` vs. `APIClient`:** `APIRequestFactory` requires you to manually authenticate each request, whereas `APIClient` allows you to set authentication once for all subsequent requests.
* **`APIRequestFactory` limitations:** When using `APIRequestFactory`, the object returned is a standard Django `HttpRequest`. Setting attributes like `.user` directly on this object will only work if `SessionAuthentication` is in use; otherwise, you must use the `force_authenticate()` helper function.
* **State management:** If you reuse the same user instance across multiple tests that update the user's state, call `refresh_from_db()` between tests.

When testing views directly using a request factory, it's often convenient to be able to directly authenticate the request, rather than having to construct the correct authentication credentials.

To forcibly authenticate a request, use the
`force_authenticate()`
method.

```
`fromrest_framework.testimportforce_authenticate
factory=APIRequestFactory()user=User.objects.get(username='olivia')view=AccountDetail.as_view()# Make an authenticated request to the view...request=factory.get('/accounts/django-superstars/')force_authenticate(request,user=user)response=view(request)`
```

The signature for the method is
`force_authenticate(request, user=None, token=None)`
.  When making the call, either or both of the user and token may be set.

For example, when forcibly authenticating using a token, you might do something like the following:

```
`user=User.objects.get(username='olivia')request=factory.get('/accounts/django-superstars/')force_authenticate(request,user=user,token=user.auth_token)`
```

Note
`force_authenticate`
directly sets
`request.user`
to the in-memory
`user`
instance. If you are reusing the same
`user`
instance across multiple tests that update the saved
`user`
state, you may need to call
refresh_from_db() (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/models/instances/#django.db.models.Model.refresh_from_db)
between tests.

Note
When using
`APIRequestFactory`
, the object that is returned is Django's standard
`HttpRequest`
, and not REST framework's
`Request`
object, which is only generated once the view is called.
This means that setting attributes directly on the request object may not always have the effect you expect.  For example, setting
`.token`
directly will have no effect, and setting
`.user`
directly will only work if session authentication is being used.
```
`# Request will only authenticate if `SessionAuthentication` is in use.request=factory.get('/accounts/django-superstars/')request.user=user
response=view(request)`
```

```
`classDummyView(APIView):...factory=APIRequestFactory()request=factory.get('/',{'demo':'test'})drf_request=DummyView().initialize_request(request)assertdrf_request.query_params=={'demo':['test']}request=factory.post('/',{'example':'test'})drf_request=DummyView().initialize_request(request)assertdrf_request.data.get('example')=='test'`
```

This can be a useful shortcut if you're testing the API but don't want to have to construct valid authentication credentials in order to make test requests.

```
`user=User.objects.get(username='lauren')client=APIClient()client.force_authenticate(user=user)`
```

To unauthenticate subsequent requests, call
`force_authenticate`
setting the user and/or token to
`None`
.

```

```

*   **Fully qualified URLs:** Unlike Django's `reverse`, which returns a path, DRF's `reverse` returns a fully qualified URL by using the request to determine the host and port.

user_input: What does @api_view do to a plain function view?
reference: It wraps the function so it gets a DRF Request and returns a DRF Response for the listed HTTP methods; by default only GET is accepted and others get a 405.
reference_contexts: By default only GET methods will be accepted. Other methods will respond with "405 Method Not Allowed".
llm_response:
The `@api_view` decorator transforms a plain function view by providing the following functionality:

*   **Request/Response handling:** It ensures the view receives a `Request` instance (instead of a standard Django `HttpRequest`) and allows the view to return a `Response` object (instead of a Django `HttpResponse`).
*   **Method restriction:** It allows you to specify which HTTP methods the view responds to via the `http_method_names` argument (defaulting to `['GET']`). If a request is made using a method not included in this list, the decorator returns a `405 Method Not Allowed` response.
*   **Configuration:** It allows you to configure how the request is processed and uses the default renderers, parsers, and authentication classes specified in the settings.
*   **Context and Error Handling:** It adds context to `Response` objects to enable content negotiation and handles `ParseError` exceptions that occur when accessing `request.data` with malformed input.

The
`@api_view`
decorator for working with function based views.
The
`APIView`

`Request`
instances in your view, and adding context to
`Response`
objects so that content negotiation can be performed.

The wrappers also provide behavior such as returning

I want each user to authenticate once and then send some credential on every request, and I need an endpoint that hands that credential back given a username and password. What's the DRF-native approach and what do I have to install/migrate?
reference: TokenAuthentication fits client-server setups like mobile apps. Enable it plus rest_framework.authtoken, run migrate, and expose the built-in obtain_auth_token view so clients POST username/password and get a token to send in the Authorization header.
reference_contexts: Token authentication is appropriate for client-server setups, such as native desktop and mobile clients.
REST framework provides a built-in view to provide this behavior.

The obtain_auth_token view will return a JSON response when valid username and password fields are POSTed to the view using form data or JSON: { 'token' : '9944b09199c62bcf9418ad846dd0e4bbdfc6ee4b' } Note that the default obtain_auth_token view explicitly uses JSON requests and responses, rather than using default renderer and parser classes in your settings.

llm_response:
The DRF-native approach for token-based authentication is `TokenAuthentication`.

### Installation and Configuration
To implement this, you must perform the following steps:

1.  **Add to `INSTALLED_APPS`**: Include `rest_framework.authtoken` in your `INSTALLED_APPS` setting:
    ```python
    INSTALLED_APPS = [
        ...
        'rest_framework.authtoken'
    ]
    ```
2.  **Run Migrations**: Execute `python manage.py migrate` to create the necessary database tables for tokens.
3.  **Configure Authentication Classes**: Set `TokenAuthentication` in your `DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES` within your `REST_FRAMEWORK` settings:
    ```python
    REST_FRAMEWORK = {
        'DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES': [
            'rest_framework.authentication.TokenAuthentication',
        ]
    }
    ```

### Endpoint for Credentials
To provide an endpoint that returns a token given a username and password, add the built-in `obtain_auth_token` view to your `urls.py`:

```python
from rest_framework.authtoken import views
urlpatterns += [path('api-token-auth/', views.obtain_auth_token)]
```

### Important Considerations
*   **Security**: If you use `TokenAuthentication` in production, you must ensure your API is only available over `https`.
*   **Alternatives**: The documentation notes that `TokenAuthentication` is a simple implementation. For more advanced requirements (such as multiple tokens per user, token expiry, or tighter security), it recommends the third-party package **Django REST Knox**. Another alternative for token-based authentication that does not require a database to validate tokens is **JSON Web Token (JWT)**, available via the `djangorestframework-simplejwt` package.

Authentication - Django REST framework

Authentication

Auth needs to be pluggable.
— Jacob Kaplan-Moss,
"REST worst practices" (https://jacobian.org/writing/rest-worst-practices/)

Authentication is the mechanism of associating an incoming request with a set of identifying credentials, such as the user the request came from, or the token that it was signed with.  The
permission (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/permissions/)
and
throttling (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/throttling/)
policies can then use those credentials to determine if the request should be permitted.

REST framework provides several authentication schemes out of the box, and also allows you to implement custom schemes.

Authentication always runs at the very start of the view, before the permission and throttling checks occur, and before any other code is allowed to proceed.

The
`request.user`
property will typically be set to an instance of the
`contrib.auth`
package's
`User`
class.

The
`request.auth`
property is used for any additional authentication information, for example, it may be used to represent an authentication token that the request was signed with.

Note
Don't forget that
authentication by itself won't allow or disallow an incoming request
, it simply identifies the credentials that the request was made with.
For information on how to set up the permission policies for your API please see the
permissions documentation (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/permissions/)
.

Note
The token authentication provided by Django REST framework is a fairly simple implementation.
For an implementation which allows more than one token per user, has some tighter security implementation details, and supports token expiry, please see the
Django REST Knox (https://github.com/James1345/django-rest-knox)
third party package.

This authentication scheme uses a simple token-based HTTP Authentication scheme.  Token authentication is appropriate for client-server setups, such as native desktop and mobile clients.

To use the
`TokenAuthentication`
scheme you'll need to
configure the authentication classes (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/authentication/#setting-the-authentication-scheme)
to include
`TokenAuthentication`
, and additionally include
`rest_framework.authtoken`
in your
`INSTALLED_APPS`
setting:

```
`INSTALLED_APPS=[...'rest_framework.authtoken']`
```

Make sure to run
`manage.py migrate`
after changing your settings.

The
`rest_framework.authtoken`
app provides Django database migrations.

You'll also need to create tokens for your users.

```
`fromrest_framework.authtoken.modelsimportTokentoken=Token.objects.create(user=...)print(token.key)`
```

For clients to authenticate, the token key should be included in the
`Authorization`
HTTP header.  The key should be prefixed by the string literal "Token", with whitespace separating the two strings.  For example:

```
`Authorization:Token9944b09199c62bcf9418ad846dd0e4bbdfc6ee4b`
```

If you want to use a different keyword in the header, such as
`Bearer`
, simply subclass
`TokenAuthentication`
and set the
`keyword`
class variable.

If successfully authenticated,
`TokenAuthentication`
provides the following credentials.

`request.user`
will be a Django
`User`
instance.
`request.auth`
will be a
`rest_framework.authtoken.models.Token`
instance.

Unauthenticated responses that are denied permission will result in an
`HTTP 401 Unauthorized`
response with an appropriate WWW-Authenticate header.  For example:

```
`WWW-Authenticate:Token`
```

The
`curl`
command line tool may be useful for testing token authenticated APIs.  For example:

```
`curl-X GET http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/example/ -H 'Authorization: Token 9944b09199c62bcf9418ad846dd0e4bbdfc6ee4b'`
```

Note
If you use
`TokenAuthentication`
in production you must ensure that your API is only available over
`https`
.

When using
`TokenAuthentication`
, you may want to provide a mechanism for clients to obtain a token given the username and password.  REST framework provides a built-in view to provide this behavior.  To use it, add the
`obtain_auth_token`
view to your URLconf:

```
`fromrest_framework.authtokenimportviews
urlpatterns+=[path('api-token-auth/',views.obtain_auth_token)]`
```

Note that the URL part of the pattern can be whatever you want to use.

The
`obtain_auth_token`
view will return a JSON response when valid
`username`
and
`password`
fields are POSTed to the view using form data or JSON:

```
`{'token':'9944b09199c62bcf9418ad846dd0e4bbdfc6ee4b'}`
```

Note that the default
`obtain_auth_token`
view explicitly uses JSON requests and responses, rather than using default renderer and parser classes in your settings.

By default, there are no permissions or throttling applied to the
`obtain_auth_token`
view. If you do wish to apply throttling you'll need to override the view class,
and include them using the
`throttle_classes`
attribute.

If you need a customized version of the
`obtain_auth_token`
view, you can do so by subclassing the
`ObtainAuthToken`
view class, and using that in your url conf instead.

For example, you may return additional user information beyond the
`token`
value:

```
`fromrest_framework.authtoken.viewsimportObtainAuthTokenfromrest_framework.authtoken.modelsimportTokenfromrest_framework.responseimportResponseclassCustomAuthToken(ObtainAuthToken):defpost(self,request,*args,**kwargs):serializer=self.serializer_class(data=request.data,context={'request':request})serializer.is_valid(raise_exception=True)user=serializer.validated_data['user']token,created=Token.objects.get_or_create(user=user)returnResponse({'token':token.key,'user_id':user.pk,'email':user.email})`
```

And in your
`urls.py`
:

```
`urlpatterns+=[path('api-token-auth/',CustomAuthToken.as_view())]`
```

The default authentication schemes may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
setting.  For example.

```
`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES':['rest_framework.authentication.BasicAuthentication','rest_framework.authentication.SessionAuthentication',]}`
```

You can also set the authentication scheme on a per-view or per-viewset basis,
using the
`APIView`
class-based views.

```
`fromrest_framework.authenticationimportSessionAuthentication,BasicAuthenticationfromrest_framework.permissionsimportIsAuthenticatedfromrest_framework.responseimportResponsefromrest_framework.viewsimportAPIViewclassExampleView(APIView):authentication_classes=[SessionAuthentication,BasicAuthentication]permission_classes=[IsAuthenticated]defget(self,request,format=None):content={'user':str(request.user),# `django.contrib.auth.User` instance.'auth':str(request.auth),# None}returnResponse(content)`
```

Or, if you're using the
`@api_view`
decorator with function based views.

```
`@api_view(['GET'])@authentication_classes([SessionAuthentication,BasicAuthentication])@permission_classes([IsAuthenticated])defexample_view(request,format=None):content={'user':str(request.user),# `django.contrib.auth.User` instance.'auth':str(request.auth),# None}returnResponse(content)`
```

JSON Web Token is a fairly new standard which can be used for token-based authentication. Unlike the built-in TokenAuthentication scheme, JWT Authentication doesn't need to use a database to validate a token. A package for JWT authentication is
djangorestframework-simplejwt (https://github.com/davesque/django-rest-framework-simplejwt)
which provides some features as well as a pluggable token blacklist app.

Django-rest-knox (https://github.com/James1345/django-rest-knox)
library provides models and views to handle token-based authentication in a more secure and extensible way than the built-in TokenAuthentication scheme - with Single Page Applications and Mobile clients in mind. It provides per-client tokens, and views to generate them when provided some other authentication (usually basic authentication), to delete the token (providing a server enforced logout) and to delete all tokens (logs out all clients that a user is logged into).

user_input: I want everyone to be able to browse my data, but only the user who created a record should be able to change or delete it. How do I structure this in DRF?
reference: Combine IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly with a custom object-level permission (IsOwnerOrReadOnly) whose has_object_permission allows safe methods for anyone and write methods only when obj.owner == request.user.
reference_contexts: BasePermission ): """ Custom permission to only allow owners of an object to edit it.
SAFE_METHODS : return True # Write permissions are only allowed to the owner of the snippet.
The IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly will allow authenticated users to perform any request.
llm_response:
To allow everyone to browse data while restricting update and delete actions to the record's creator, follow these steps:

### 1. Associate Users with Records
Ensure your model instances are associated with a user. In your view class (e.g., `SnippetList`), override the `.perform_create()` method to save the owner during creation:

```python
def perform_create(self, serializer):
    serializer.save(owner=self.request.user)
```

### 2. Create a Custom Permission Class
Create a file named `permissions.py` and define a class that inherits from `permissions.BasePermission`. Implement the `has_object_permission` method to allow read-only access for all users and restrict write access to the owner:

```python
from rest_framework import permissions

class IsOwnerOrReadOnly(permissions.BasePermission):
    """Custom permission to only allow owners of an object to edit it."""
    def has_object_permission(self, request, view, obj):
        # Read permissions are allowed to any request (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS)
        if request.method in permissions.SAFE_METHODS:
            return True
        # Write permissions are only allowed to the owner
        return obj.owner == request.user
```

### 3. Apply the Permission to the View
Add the custom permission to the `permission_classes` property of your detail view class (e.g., `SnippetDetail`):

```python
from snippets.permissions import IsOwnerOrReadOnly
from rest_framework import permissions

permission_classes = [permissions.IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly, IsOwnerOrReadOnly]
```

### Important Implementation Notes:
*   **Generic Views:** If you are using generic views, object-level permissions are handled automatically.
*   **Custom Views:** If you are writing your own custom views, you must manually call `self.check_object_permissions(request, obj)` once you have the object instance to trigger the permission check.
*   **List Views:** Object-level permissions are only checked for views that retrieve a single instance. If you need to filter list views, you must handle that separately via queryset filtering.

reference: Don't take it from request data. In a generic view override perform_create to save with user=self.request.user, or on the serializer use a HiddenField with default=CurrentUserDefault so the current user is injected at save.
reference_contexts: These hooks are particularly useful for setting attributes that are implicit in the request, but are not part of the request data.
A default class that can be used to represent the current user.
This field will be present in validated_data but will not be used in the serializer output representation.
llm_response:
To set the owner automatically to the logged-in user without the client sending it, you can use one of the following two approaches:

### 1. Using `HiddenField` and `CurrentUserDefault` (Recommended for field-level defaults)
This approach uses a `HiddenField`, which is present in `validated_data` but excluded from the API's output representation, ensuring the client does not send it.

Add this to your serializer:
```python
owner = serializers.HiddenField(default=serializers.CurrentUserDefault())
```
**Requirement:** You must provide the `request` in the context dictionary when instantiating the serializer.

### 2. Overriding `.perform_create()` (Recommended for view-level logic)
If you prefer to handle the association in the view, you can override the `.perform_create()` method. This allows you to inject the user from the request into the save process.

Add this method to your view class:
```python
def perform_create(self, serializer):
    serializer.save(owner=self.request.user)
```
When using this method, the `create()` method of your serializer will receive the `'owner'` field along with the validated data.

***

**Note on Serializer Representation:**
To display the owner in the API output (while keeping it read-only for the client), use a `ReadOnlyField` in your serializer:
```python
owner = serializers.ReadOnlyField(source="owner.username")
```
This field will be used for serialized representations but will not be used when deserializing or updating model instances.

user_input: My API is getting hammered. I want to cap how many requests anonymous vs logged-in users can make per day. What's the mechanism and where do the numbers go?
reference: Enable AnonRateThrottle and UserRateThrottle as throttle classes and put the actual limits (like '100/day' and '1000/day') under DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES.
reference_contexts: The default throttling policy may be set globally, using the DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES and DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES settings.

REST_FRAMEWORK = { 'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES' : [ 'rest_framework.throttling.AnonRateThrottle' , 'rest_framework.throttling.UserRateThrottle' ], 'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES' : { 'anon' : '100/day' , 'user' : '1000/day' } } The rates used in DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES can be specified over a period of second, minute, hour or day.
A list or tuple of throttle classes, that determines the default set of throttles checked at the start of a view.
llm_response:
To cap requests for anonymous and logged-in users, you should use the built-in `AnonRateThrottle` and `UserRateThrottle` classes.

### The Mechanism
The recommended approach is to set these globally in your project's `REST_FRAMEWORK` settings. You must include both classes in `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES` and define their limits in `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`.

### Where the Numbers Go
You define the rates within the `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES` dictionary in your settings file. The keys `'anon'` and `'user'` correspond to the respective throttle classes.

**Example configuration:**
```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES': [
        'rest_framework.throttling.AnonRateThrottle',
        'rest_framework.throttling.UserRateThrottle'
    ],
    'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES': {
        'anon': '100/day',
        'user': '1000/day'
    }
}
```

### Rate Format
The rates are specified as a string containing the number of requests followed by a period (e.g., `/day`). You can use `s`, `m`, `h`, or `d` to represent seconds, minutes, hours, or days.

### Additional Notes
*   **Cache Requirement:** Throttling relies on Django's cache framework. Ensure you have appropriate cache settings configured; the default `LocMemCache` is sufficient for simple setups.
*   **Per-View Overrides:** While global settings are recommended, you can override these on a per-view or per-viewset basis by setting the `throttle_classes` attribute on your `APIView` or using the `@throttle_classes` decorator for function-based views.
*   **Scope:** `AnonRateThrottle` uses the request's IP address to track limits. `UserRateThrottle` uses the user ID, falling back to the IP address for unauthenticated requests.

Throttling is similar to
permissions (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/permissions/)
, in that it determines if a request should be authorized.  Throttles indicate a temporary state, and are used to control the rate of requests that clients can make to an API.

As with permissions, multiple throttles may be used.  Your API might have a restrictive throttle for unauthenticated requests, and a less restrictive throttle for authenticated requests.

Another scenario where you might want to use multiple throttles would be if you need to impose different constraints on different parts of the API, due to some services being particularly resource-intensive.

Multiple throttles can also be used if you want to impose both burst throttling rates, and sustained throttling rates.  For example, you might want to limit a user to a maximum of 60 requests per minute, and 1000 requests per day.

Throttles do not necessarily only refer to rate-limiting requests.  For example a storage service might also need to throttle against bandwidth, and a paid data service might want to throttle against a certain number of a records being accessed.

The application-level throttling that REST framework provides should not be considered a security measure or protection against brute forcing or denial-of-service attacks. To handle slow or down payment provider exceptions globally and return a machine-readable response, you should implement a custom exception handler. This allows you to define the error response logic once rather than repeating it in every view.

### Implementation Steps

1.  **Create a custom handler function**: Define a function that accepts the exception (`exc`) and the context (`context`). This function should check for your specific payment provider exception, return a `Response` object with your desired JSON structure (e.g., `{"detail": "try again shortly"}`), and fall back to the default handler for other exceptions.

    ```python
    from rest_framework.views import exception_handler
    from rest_framework.response import Response

    def custom_exception_handler(exc, context):
        # Call REST framework's default exception handler first
        response = exception_handler(exc, context)

        # Check for your specific payment provider exception here
        if isinstance(exc, YourPaymentProviderException):
            return Response({"detail": "try again shortly"}, status=503)

        return response
    ```

2.  **Configure the setting**: Register your handler in your project's settings file using the `EXCEPTION_HANDLER` key:

    ```python
    REST_FRAMEWORK = {
        'EXCEPTION_HANDLER': 'my_project.my_app.utils.custom_exception_handler'
    }
    ```

### Important Considerations
*   **Scope**: The exception handler is only triggered for responses generated by raised exceptions. It will not be used for responses returned directly by a view.
*   **Generic 500 Errors**: If you also want to ensure that unhandled server errors return JSON instead of HTML, you can set `handler500` in your URL configuration to `rest_framework.exceptions.server_error`:
    ```python
    handler500 = 'rest_framework.exceptions.server_error'
    ```
    This provides a generic JSON 500 response, which is more appropriate for API-only applications than Django's default HTML error views.

To avoid creating parallel serializers and endpoints, you can dynamically modify the fields returned by your serializer. The documentation provides two primary approaches:

### 1. Built-in Custom Implementation (Recommended)
You can create a custom serializer class that accepts a `fields` argument at initialization to filter the output. This allows you to control the response fields at the point of instantiation without needing external dependencies.

Define a `DynamicFieldsModelSerializer` as follows:

```python
class DynamicFieldsModelSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    """
    A ModelSerializer that takes an additional `fields` argument that
    controls which fields should be displayed.
    """
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        # Don't pass the 'fields' arg up to the superclass
        fields = kwargs.pop('fields', None)
        # Instantiate the superclass normally
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        if fields is not None:
            # Drop any fields that are not specified in the `fields` argument.
            allowed = set(fields)
            existing = set(self.fields)
            for field_name in existing - allowed:
                self.fields.pop(field_name)
```

You can then use this class in your views to return only the required columns for the mobile client while returning the full object for the web client.

### 2. Third-Party Packages
If you prefer not to maintain custom code, several third-party packages provide dynamic field selection:

*   **[drf-dynamic-fields](https://github.com/dbrgn/drf-dynamic-fields):** Provides a mixin to limit fields based on a URL parameter.
*   **[djangorestframework-queryfields](https://djangorestframework-queryfields.readthedocs.io/):** Allows clients to specify fields via inclusion/exclusion query parameters.
*   **[drf-flex-fields](https://github.com/rsinger86/drf-flex-fields):** Extends `ModelSerializer` and `ModelViewSet` to set fields dynamically from URL parameters or class definitions.
*   **[django-rest-framework-serializer-extensions](https://github.com/evenicoulddoit/django-rest-framework-serializer-extensions):** Allows fields to be defined on a per-view/request basis (whitelisting/blacklisting).
*   **[drf-shapeless-serializers](https://github.com/khaledsukkar2/drf-shapeless-serializers):** Provides runtime field selection and configuration without creating multiple serializer classes.

**Recommendation:** Use the built-in `DynamicFieldsModelSerializer` approach (Excerpt 1) as it is a native implementation that avoids external dependencies while directly addressing your requirement to avoid parallel serializers.

llm_response:
To set up a self-describing API that you can click around in a browser while maintaining JSON as the primary format, use the **Django REST framework**.

### Setting up the Browsable API
The framework provides a "Browsable API" that generates human-friendly HTML output for your resources, allowing you to browse them and submit data via `POST`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` forms.

1.  **Automatic Routing:** Use a `Router` class (such as `DefaultRouter`) to automatically wire up your resources. This also creates an API root view for you.
    ```python
    from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter
    from snippets import views

    router = DefaultRouter()
    router.register(r"snippets", views.SnippetViewSet, basename="snippet")
    router.register(r"users", views.UserViewSet, basename="user")

    urlpatterns = [
        path("", include(router.urls)),
    ]
    ```
2.  **Self-Description:** The API becomes self-describing by adding docstrings to your views or viewsets. These docstrings are automatically rendered in the browsable interface. If the `Markdown` library is installed, you can use markdown syntax in these docstrings to format the documentation.

### Managing Formats
The API is designed to handle multiple formats:
*   **Browser Default:** By default, the API detects the browser and returns the HTML-based browsable interface.
*   **JSON Primary:** Because the API is format-negotiated, you can access the raw JSON response in your browser at any time by appending `?format=json` to the URL. 
*   **Tooling:** For a better experience when viewing JSON in the browser, the documentation recommends using JSON-viewing extensions for Firefox or Chrome.

llm_response:
To eliminate boilerplate URL patterns, you should use **ViewSets** in combination with a **Router**.

### 1. Use ViewSets
Instead of writing separate views for list and detail actions, combine the logic for a set of related views into a single `ViewSet` class. A `ViewSet` provides actions like `.list()` and `.create()` rather than method handlers like `.get()` or `.post()`.

### 2. Use a Router
Rather than explicitly registering views in your `urls.py`, use a `Router` class to automatically determine the URL configuration.

**Recommended Approach:**
Use `DefaultRouter`, which automatically handles the URL configuration and creates an API root view for you.

**Implementation Steps:**
1.  **Instantiate the router:** Create an instance of `DefaultRouter`.
2.  **Register your ViewSets:** Use the `router.register()` method, providing the URL prefix and the viewset class.
3.  **Include the URLs:** Add `router.urls` to your `urlpatterns`.

**Example:**
```python
from django.urls import path, include
from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter
from snippets import views

# Create a router and register our ViewSets with it.
router = DefaultRouter()
router.register(r"snippets", views.SnippetViewSet, basename="snippet")
router.register(r"users", views.UserViewSet, basename="user")

# The API URLs are now determined automatically by the router.
urlpatterns = [
    path("", include(router.urls)),
]
```

### Important Notes:
*   **`basename`:** This argument is used to specify the initial part of the URL name pattern (e.g., `'snippet-list'`, `'snippet-detail'`). You typically do not need to set it if your viewset has a `.queryset` attribute. However, if you have defined a custom `get_queryset` method and the viewset lacks a `.queryset` attribute, you must explicitly provide the `basename` argument to avoid an error.
*   **Alternative:** You can also use `SimpleRouter` if you do not require the automatic API root view provided by `DefaultRouter`.

reference: That dropdown is built from the relational field's `choices`, and the browsable rendering of relational fields is already capped — by default it renders at most 1000 selectable items and then shows a disabled 'More than 1000 items…' entry. html_cutoff - If set this will be the maximum number of choices that will be displayed by a HTML select drop down. Set to None to disable any limiting. Defaults to 1000.

llm_response:
To address the performance issue caused by rendering 80,000 rows in a dropdown, you have the following options:

**1. Use the `html_cutoff` argument**
You can limit the number of choices displayed in the HTML select dropdown. By setting `html_cutoff` to a lower value (the default is 1000), you prevent the browser from attempting to render all 80,000 rows. When the limit is reached, the browsable API will display a disabled option indicating that items have been cut off. You can customize this text using the `html_cutoff_text` argument.

**2. Use a plain input field**
If you prefer not to use a dropdown, you can change the field to a plain input field by using the `style` keyword argument. This is done by setting the `base_template` to `'input.html'`:

```python
assigned_to = serializers.SlugRelatedField(
    queryset=User.objects.all(),
    slug_field='username',
    style={'base_template': 'input.html'}
)
```

**Global Configuration**
If you wish to apply these limits across your entire project rather than on a specific field, you can use the global settings `HTML_SELECT_CUTOFF` and `HTML_SELECT_CUTOFF_TEXT`.

When rendered in the browsable API relational fields will default to only displaying a maximum of 1000 selectable items. If more items are present then a disabled option with "More than 1000 items…" will be displayed.

`None`

.
